title: Relation Between Stress and Strain
short_intro: Stress is defined as the internal restoring force per unit area set up inside a deformed body, while strain is the fractional change in dimension resulting from that stress. Hooke's law establishes a linear proportionality between stress and strain within the elastic limit of a material.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of stress and strain, types of stress (longitudinal, shearing, volumetric), Hooke's law, elastic moduli (Young's modulus, bulk modulus, modulus of rigidity), and basic numerical problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Inter-relations between elastic constants (Y, K, η, σ), Poisson's ratio limits (-1 to 0.5), stored elastic potential energy per unit volume, strain energy in twisted cylinders, and thermal stresses.

prerequisites: Dimensions and dimensional formulas of mechanical quantities
Forces in equilibrium and Newton's laws of motion
Basic vector and tensor concepts for advanced PGT stress analysis

concept_notes.heading: Concept of Stress
bullets: Stress is a tensor quantity measured as force per unit cross-sectional area, F/A.
Normal stress acts perpendicular to the surface (causing elongation or compression), whereas tangential or shearing stress acts parallel to the surface.
SI unit of stress is N/m² or Pascal (Pa) with dimensional formula [ML<sup>-1</sup>T<sup>-2</sup>].

concept_notes.heading: Concept of Strain
bullets: Strain is a dimensionless and unitless quantity representing the relative deformation of a body.
Longitudinal strain is ΔL/L, volumetric strain is ΔV/V, and shearing strain is θ or tan θ ≈ Δx/l.
It expresses how much a given body is deformed relative to its original configuration.

concept_notes.heading: Hooke's Law and Elastic Moduli
bullets: Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain, meaning Stress = E × Strain, where E is the modulus of elasticity.
Young's modulus (Y) governs longitudinal deformation, Bulk modulus (K) governs volumetric compression, and Rigidity modulus (η) governs shape change under shear.
The reciprocal of bulk modulus is known as compressibility.

concept_notes.heading: Poisson's Ratio and Elastic Constants Interrelation
bullets: Poisson's ratio (σ) is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain under uniaxial stress.
Theoretical isotropic limits for Poisson's ratio are -1 to 0.5, while practical materials exhibit values between 0 and 0.5.

derivations.title: Derivation of Elastic Potential Energy Density
derivations.conditions: Isotropic, linearly elastic material stressed within the proportional limit
steps: Consider a wire of original length L and cross-sectional area A subjected to a variable stretching force F.
The incremental work done in stretching the wire by an infinitesimal length dl is dW = F dl.
Substitute F = (YA/L)l into the work integral from l = 0 to l = ΔL.
Divide by volume (V = AL) to obtain energy density U = (1/2) × Stress × Strain.

derivations.title: Relation between Young's Modulus, Bulk Modulus, and Modulus of Rigidity
steps: Write the independent constitutive relations linking Young's modulus Y, Bulk modulus K, and Rigidity modulus η.
Use Poisson's ratio σ to eliminate lateral strain components from volumetric and shear strain equations.
Substitute σ back into either Y = 3K(1 - 2σ) or Y = 2η(1 + σ).
Obtain the master relation connecting all three moduli: \frac{9}{Y} = \frac{1}{K} + \frac{3}{\eta}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stress-Strain Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of Stress (y-axis) versus Strain (x-axis) showing proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The linear region represents Hooke's law validity. Beyond the yield point, permanent plastic deformation occurs leading up to necking and fracture.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification questions on ductile vs. brittle materials and the exact definitions of yield and breaking stress.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's Apparatus Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup featuring two long parallel wires (experimental and reference), a spirit level, a micrometer screw gauge, and added dead weights.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine Young's modulus of a metallic wire accurately by measuring small elongations for known loads.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions on least count, error propagation, and formula application for Y.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Compressibility Measurement via Bulk Modulus
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Graph of fractional volume change (ΔV/V) versus applied uniform pressure (ΔP).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the linear graph yields the inverse of the bulk modulus, which is the compressibility factor.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on fluids and solids under high hydrostatic pressure.

solved_numericals.question: A steel wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 mm² is pulled by a force of 200 N. If Young's modulus of steel is 2 × 10¹¹ N/m², calculate the elongation produced in the wire.
solution_steps: Identify given values: L = 2 m, A = 1 mm² = 1 × 10&sup-;&sup6; m², F = 200 N, Y = 2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
Rearrange Young's modulus formula for elongation: ΔL = \frac{FL}{YA}.

solved_numericals.question: For a given isotropic material, the Young's modulus is equal to its bulk modulus. Find the Poisson's ratio of the material.
solution_steps: State the relation connecting Young's modulus, bulk modulus, and Poisson's ratio: Y = 3K(1 - 2σ).
Substitute the given condition Y = K into the equation: K = 3K(1 - 2σ).
Divide both sides by K (since K ≠ 0): 1 = 3(1 - 2σ).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the elastic potential energy stored per unit volume in a copper wire subject to a longitudinal stress of 4 × 10&sup7; N/m². Take Young's modulus of copper as 1.2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
solution_steps: Identify given values: Stress σ = 4 × 10&sup7; N/m², Y = 1.2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
Use the energy density formula in terms of stress and Young's modulus: u = \frac{\sigma^2}{2Y}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Hooke's law is strictly valid only within the proportional limit of the stress-strain curve.
Materials are assumed to be perfectly homogeneous and isotropic for standard elastic constant inter-relations.
Deformations are assumed to be small so that higher-order nonlinear strain terms can be neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Strain has SI units of percentage or ratio dimensions like meters.
common_misconceptions.correct: Strain is strictly a dimensionless quantity.
common_misconceptions.why: It is the ratio of two like quantities (change in dimension to original dimension).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Poisson's ratio can take any positive value up to infinity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Poisson's ratio for stable isotropic materials lies strictly between -1 and 0.5.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermodynamic stability requirements dictate that bulk and shear moduli must remain positive.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A stiffer material has a lower Young's modulus.
common_misconceptions.correct: A higher Young's modulus indicates greater stiffness.
common_misconceptions.why: Modulus is the slope of the stress-strain curve; higher slope means less deformation for the same applied stress.

quick_revision: Stress is restoring force per unit area (N/m²), while strain is fractional deformation (dimensionless).
Hooke's law states Stress = E × Strain within the elastic limit.
Young's modulus (Y), Bulk modulus (K), and Rigidity modulus (η) characterize tensile, volumetric, and shear elasticity respectively.
Poisson's ratio σ relates lateral strain to longitudinal strain with theoretical bounds of -1 to 0.5.
